passage: Arnab got off the bus at Chandipur at noon, two days after landing from his exchange semester in California. His cousin Yogesh was waiting with the scooter. By evening Arnab had fallen asleep in the middle of Thakuma's welcome meal, head nodding over the rice. At two in the morning he was wide awake, listening to frogs and staring at the ceiling fan. The next day he forgot where he had put his passport and shouted at Yogesh for moving it. It was in his own bag. Yogesh only said, 'Come, let's go to the fields.' They walked the paddy bunds in the early sun, then helped with the cows. Arnab stayed up until the village went quiet that night. Each day after, the fog in his head thinned a little.

qa.q: Where did Arnab and Yogesh walk the next day?
qa.a: They walked the paddy bunds in the early sun.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he shouted at Yogesh about the passport?
qa.a: He felt foggy, frustrated and irritable from the long journey, so he blamed Yogesh even though the passport was in his own bag.

qa.q: What worked in Yogesh's response?
qa.a: Instead of arguing, Yogesh took Arnab out in the early sun and kept him busy with the cows, helping his body settle into village time.

qa.q: What was it like for Yogesh to be shouted at over the passport?
qa.a: It was unfair and probably stung, but Yogesh seemed to understand that Arnab was worn out and chose patience over a quarrel.

grounding: Shows a student back from a flight across many time zones who is sleepy at odd hours, forgetful and irritable, and adjusts with morning daylight, activity and patience.

passage: Thanks, Francis. So I'm Ujjwal, and my first week in Toronto was a mess. I flew twenty-two hours from Kolkata, landed at night, and my body thought it was morning. I'd be wide awake at three a.m., then at orientation I nodded off in the middle of the dean's welcome. I forgot my room key twice and snapped at my roommate over a towel. I kept thinking something was wrong with me. A senior said: get outside in the morning light, eat at local mealtimes, and give it a few days. So I walked by the lake every morning, even feeling like a zombie. By the second week I was sleeping at night like a normal person again.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal walk every morning?
qa.a: By the lake.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal worried about during the first week?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt worried that something was wrong, being so sleepy at odd hours, forgetful and snappy.

qa.q: What advice from the senior helped?
qa.a: Getting morning light, eating at local mealtimes and giving the body a few days to adjust.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal's roommate have felt about the towel argument?
qa.a: The roommate may have felt puzzled or hurt, not knowing the snappiness came from jet lag.

grounding: A student after a long flight feels sleepy at odd hours, forgetful and irritable, and daylight plus patience help.

passage:
Day one: Ritu landed in Bhopal from London at dawn and was wide awake at midnight, unpacking. At breakfast she was so sleepy she poured tea into the sugar bowl, and she snapped when her brother Pradeep laughed.
Day three: At four in the afternoon Ritu was dozing on the sofa again. Pradeep shook her awake. 'Don't nap now. Sit on the terrace in the morning sun,' he said. Next morning she took her tea out into the sunlight, and that night she stayed awake till ten.
Day six: Ritu went to the market with Pradeep, remembered everything on Ma's list, and laughed about the sugar bowl.

qa.q: What did Ritu pour tea into?
qa.a: The sugar bowl.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel when Pradeep laughed at breakfast?
qa.a: She felt irritable and embarrassed; the jet lag had made her sleepy and short-tempered.

qa.q: What helped Ritu's body adjust?
qa.a: Skipping the afternoon nap and sitting in the morning sun, with a few days of patience.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have seen Ritu's snapping on day one?
qa.a: He may have felt a little stung, but he guessed it was jet lag and helped her adjust.

grounding: Over several days a student back from abroad is sleepy and irritable until morning daylight and patience reset her body clock.

passage: Bidisha, you are grumbling about jet lag before you've even packed! Sit, let your Anirban Jethu tell you something. In ninety-four I flew to Munich for my master's, my first time on a plane. For five days my body lived in Calcutta. I'd fall asleep in the library at noon and stare at the ceiling at three in the morning. I was so irritable that I argued with my landlady about a kettle, and I even forgot my professor's name when he greeted me. I was sure I would fail. Then my lab-mate dragged me for walks along the river every morning. Light in the morning, dinner at their dinner time, no afternoon naps. By the second week I was myself again. So be patient with your body, ma.

qa.q: Where did Anirban fly in ninety-four?
qa.a: To Munich, for his master's.

qa.q: How did young Anirban feel during those first five days?
qa.a: He felt irritable and scared he would fail, falling asleep at noon and forgetting his professor's name.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Anirban's story?
qa.a: The lab-mate taking him on morning walks by the river; morning light and local mealtimes helped his body adjust.

qa.q: How might the landlady have seen the argument over the kettle?
qa.a: She may have thought the new student was rude, not knowing jet lag had made him short-tempered.

grounding: An uncle recalls how jet lag made him sleepy, forgetful and irritable as a student, and how daylight and patience helped.

passage: Harish landed in Toronto after twenty-two hours of travel, and his suitcase didn't. For three days he wore the same hoodie and lived on the wrong clock: wide awake at 3 a.m. refreshing the missing-baggage page, then nodding off in his first lecture at eleven. He forgot his room key twice and snapped at the front desk. Sharmila, a second-year from the floor below who had made the same trip last year, knocked on his door. "Jet lag. Everyone gets it. Go outside in the morning light, eat meals at local times, keep naps short. Give it a few days." Harish grumbled, but walked the frozen lake path at nine the next morning. By Friday his suitcase had arrived, and so, mostly, had his sleep.

qa.q: What went missing on Harish's journey?
qa.a: His suitcase didn't arrive with him.

qa.q: How was Harish feeling during those first three days?
qa.a: He felt sleepy at odd hours, forgetful and irritable, and snapped at the front desk.

qa.q: What does Sharmila suggest to help his body adjust?
qa.a: Getting morning light, eating at local mealtimes, keeping naps short and being patient for a few days.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see Harish's grumpiness?
qa.a: Sharmila sees it as ordinary jet lag, remembering the same trip last year, rather than as rudeness.

grounding: Shows a student after a long flight across time zones sleepy at odd hours, forgetful and irritable, and daylight at local times plus patience helping him adjust.
